interactions: Fosphenytoin or phenytoin + dexamethasone: phenytoin induces CYP3A4 and increases dexamethasone clearance, reducing its anti-edema effect; dexamethasone can alter phenytoin concentrations; avoid the combination or monitor free phenytoin levels and clinical response
Carbamazepine + dexamethasone: CYP3A4 induction lowers dexamethasone exposure; avoid

Valproate + bevacizumab: valproate can cause thrombocytopenia and platelet dysfunction, and bevacizumab carries a risk of hemorrhage including intratumoral bleeding; monitor platelets and for bleeding
Citalopram + other QT-prolonging drugs: additive QT prolongation; baseline ECG before adding one
output.proposed: Antiseizure options (levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, valproate, lacosamide, lorazepam) against current dexamethasone, bevacizumab and citalopram
output.summary: Enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs (phenytoin, fosphenytoin, carbamazepine) accelerate dexamethasone clearance. Valproate adds a platelet effect to the bleeding risk of bevacizumab. Levetiracetam and lacosamide have no relevant pharmacokinetic interaction with these drugs.
warnings: Lorazepam: no pharmacokinetic interaction; monitor respiration and blood pressure

results.finding: Convulsive status epilepticus is treated at 5 minutes with an adequately dosed benzodiazepine [Glauser_2016].
Levetiracetam, fosphenytoin and valproate were equally effective as second-line agents for benzodiazepine-refractory convulsive status epilepticus in the ESETT trial [ESETT_2019].
Seizures continuing after both tiers are refractory and are treated with an anaesthetic infusion under continuous EEG [Brophy_2012].
Continuous EEG for at least 24 hours is recommended when consciousness does not return after convulsions stop [Brophy_2012].

output.summary: Status epilepticus is treated in tiers: a benzodiazepine first, then one of three equally effective second-line drugs, then anaesthetic infusion under continuous EEG for refractory seizures [Glauser_2016; ESETT_2019; Brophy_2012].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Levetiracetam 8 mcg/mL, below range; glucose 248 on dexamethasone; bicarbonate 19 after the convulsion; WBC 14.2; hemoglobin 11.4; sodium 138, calcium 9.1, magnesium 1.9 and creatinine 1.0 normal
action_criteria.label: Emergency laboratory work-up: glucose, CBC, electrolytes, magnesium, renal and hepatic function, levetiracetam level
action_criteria.rationale: Glucose, electrolyte, renal and hepatic derangements are reversible causes of seizures and decide the ASM and its dose; the levetiracetam level shows whether the missed dose left her subtherapeutic [Brophy_2012].

action_criteria.rationale: Excludes hemorrhage, mass or edema that would change management, and must precede any LP [Brophy_2012].

action_criteria.rationale: Persistent impaired consciousness after a focal-to-bilateral convulsive SE needs EEG confirmation of ongoing seizures; continuous monitoring for at least 24 hours [Brophy_2012]; terminology [ACNS_2021].

action_criteria.rationale: Structural SE in a known glioma: MRI shows whether the tumor and its edema have progressed, which decides steroid escalation and the oncological plan [Brophy_2012].

action_criteria.rationale: She depends on dexamethasone for peritumoral edema: an enzyme-inducing ASM would lower its exposure, which steers the second-line choice [ESETT_2019].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General evidence on tiered SE treatment

action_criteria.rationale: Background evidence only; not a clinical step [Brophy_2012].

prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform a lumbar puncture: the right frontal mass with 4 mm midline shift carries a herniation risk, and CSF adds nothing to the diagnosis.
Do not use enzyme-inducing ASMs (phenytoin, fosphenytoin, carbamazepine) when levetiracetam or lacosamide is available: they lower dexamethasone exposure.
Do not escalate to anaesthetic infusion without a goals-of-care discussion in progressive glioblastoma.
required_recommendations: Give a benzodiazepine now: IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (maximum 4 mg per dose, repeat once), or IM midazolam 10 mg without IV access [Glauser_2016].

Load a second-line ASM: IV levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (maximum 4500 mg), as her level is subtherapeutic after a missed dose, and avoid fosphenytoin because enzyme induction lowers dexamethasone exposure [ESETT_2019].

Re-escalate dexamethasone for the enlarging peritumoral edema with midline shift (for example 10 mg IV, then 4 mg every 6 hours, later tapered to the lowest effective dose), with capillary glucose monitoring and insulin for steroid hyperglycemia.
Continue video-EEG for at least 24 hours after clinical and electrographic seizure control [Brophy_2012].

Discuss goals of care early with her and her husband, with neuro-oncology and palliative care, because the glioblastoma is progressing on bevacizumab; agree in advance whether intubation and anaesthetic infusion are wanted if seizures become refractory.

avoided_actions.rationale: Lumbar puncture is contraindicated with a right frontal mass, extensive edema and 4 mm midline shift: the pressure gradient risks herniation [Tunkel_2008].
No clinical suspicion of cardiac source of embolus or cardiogenic seizure; routine echo is not indicated in SE workup absent cardiac findings.
No suspicion of arrhythmogenic syncope or cardiac comorbidity precipitating SE; routine telemetry beyond standard ICU monitoring adds cost without yield.
Amyloid PET has no role in acute SE evaluation; dementia biomarker imaging does not change acute management.
Carotid duplex is for ischemic stroke workup; SE without focal vascular suspicion does not warrant carotid imaging.
Polysomnography studies sleep disorders and has no role in the acute evaluation of status epilepticus.

patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Thompson is a 68-year-old woman with right frontal glioblastoma on bevacizumab and dexamethasone who is brought by ambulance after her husband called 911 when she developed a focal motor seizure involving the left arm that progressively spread and secondarily generalized to bilateral tonic-clonic activity. The seizure has been continuous for approximately 18 minutes. She had her most recent bevacizumab infusion 5 days ago. Her husband notes she has been increasingly fatigued and had worsening headaches over the past 10 days, which she attributed to the GBM. She missed her morning levetiracetam dose today because of nausea. Her dexamethasone was recently tapered from 8 mg/day to 4 mg/day over the past 2 weeks on oncology's instruction. She has progressive disease that has been growing despite bevacizumab. She also takes citalopram. She is right-handed.
